issues.legal_issue: A guarantor or mortgagor seeking an appeal from an order of the recovery tribunal must comply with the applicable pre-deposit requirement.
material_facts: The respondent had guaranteed repayment of a loan and mortgaged its property to secure that repayment.
After the property was auctioned, the respondent challenged the sale and sought to pursue an appeal before the appellate tribunal.
The High Court held that no pre-deposit was required because no decree had been passed and no liability fixed.
issues.conclusion: A guarantor or mortgagor who seeks an appeal must comply with the pre-deposit requirement; the appellate tribunal may reduce the deposit for recorded reasons, but cannot waive it altogether. The High Court was wrong to hold otherwise.
issues.legal_principle: Section 18 of the SARFAESI Act makes pre-deposit a condition for entertaining an appeal. Under its second and third provisos, the deposit is calculated by reference to the debt claimed by the secured creditor or determined by the DRT, whichever is less, and the DRAT may reduce it, for reasons recorded in writing, but not below 25%. Narayan Chandra Ghosh v. UCO Bank, (2011) 4 SCC 548, holds that the appeal cannot be entertained without the deposit even if the DRT has not determined the debt. A guarantor or mortgagor who has secured repayment by mortgaging property stands on the same footing as a borrower for this requirement.

predicates.appeal_from_recovery_tribunal_order: The appellant seeks appellate review of an order made by a tribunal dealing with recovery proceedings.
predicates.appellant_guaranteed_or_mortgaged_proper: The appellant guaranteed repayment of a loan or mortgaged property to secure repayment of a loan.

issues.definition: When a party who guaranteed or secured a loan seeks an appeal from a recovery tribunal order, the appeal must meet the pre-deposit condition.

issues.legal_issue: A High Court cannot direct that a mandatory pre-deposit for an appeal is unnecessary.
material_facts: The High Court rejected the respondent's petition while directing it to pursue an appeal before the DRAT without making a pre-deposit.
On review, the High Court maintained that no pre-deposit was needed where the challenged order did not pass a decree or fix liability.
The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court had interpreted the statutory appeal requirement rather than exercising its discretionary jurisdiction under Article 226.
issues.conclusion: The High Court could not dispense with the mandatory pre-deposit requirement, and its orders were set aside to the extent that they held no pre-deposit was required.
issues.legal_principle: The appeal requirement in Section 18 of the SARFAESI Act cannot be overridden by a High Court direction that contradicts it. The High Court does not have powers akin to the Supreme Court's powers under Article 142 of the Constitution and cannot issue directions contrary to law. The Court distinguished the asserted exercise of jurisdiction under Article 226 because the High Court's order rested on its interpretation of the statutory requirement.

predicates.high_court_review_proceeding: A High Court considers a challenge involving the availability or conduct of an appeal to a specialist appellate tribunal.
predicates.high_court_order_excuses_required_deposi: The High Court directs that a party need not make a deposit otherwise required before its appeal can be entertained.
predicates.appeal_procedure_requires_predeposit: The applicable appeal procedure requires a deposit as a condition for entertaining the appeal.

issues.definition: If a High Court, while considering a matter involving an appeal, excuses a deposit that the applicable appeal procedure requires, it cannot make that direction.
